title: What If You Couldn't Picture Anything in Your Mind? Millions Can't

scenes.text: What if you closed your eyes and could picture nothing at all? Millions can't, and never knew.
Try it: imagine a red apple. Most people see something. Roughly two to four percent see only black. It's called aphantasia.
The word dates from 2015. A patient lost his mind's eye after heart surgery, and when the story spread, thousands wrote in saying they had never had one.
They dream, recognise faces and remember facts. They just can't replay the picture. Many were in their thirties before they realised others could.
In one experiment people read scary stories while sensors tracked their sweat. Imaginers reacted. Aphantasics stayed flat, until they saw scary pictures.
And it isn't a disability. A co-founder of Pixar has it, and he spent his career making pictures the whole world could see.

description:
What if you closed your eyes and could picture nothing at all? For roughly 2 to 4 percent of people, that is normal. It is called aphantasia.
The term was coined in 2015 by neurologist Adam Zeman at the University of Exeter after a patient lost his mind's eye following heart surgery; thousands then came forward saying they had never had visual imagery at all. Most live ordinary lives and discover the difference by accident. A 2021 study found that aphantasics show no skin-conductance response to frightening stories, though they react normally to frightening pictures. Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull is among those with the condition.
